sg1.question: [sg1 / ambiguous] The story says developers can edit 'tool locations and sign-in', but insrc stores no secrets and sign-in stays with the tracker's CLI. This LLD makes sign-in a read-only status row plus an editable ghHost (the host gh is signed in to). Is that what 'edit sign-in' should mean, or should it be something else?
sg1.choice: Sign-in is a read-only status row computed live from gh (signed in as X, not signed in, gh not found, timed out); the only editable part is ghHost, the host gh signs in to (default github.com). No secret is stored.
sg1.rationale: Owner chose option A on 2026-10-17: satisfies 'see sign-in' with live truth and gives GitHub Enterprise users something to edit, inside the no-secrets rule.

sg2.question: [sg2 / missed] ghPath, ghHost and branchPattern are stored and shown by this story, but no story makes the gh runner or branch creation read them. Which story consumes them, so a developer who sets them sees an effect? (Candidate: an s1 follow-up for ghPath/ghHost and the handoff story s6 for branchPattern.)
sg2.rationale: Owner chose option A on 2026-10-17: s3 stores and shows ghPath, ghHost and branchPattern only; the gh runner reading ghPath and ghHost is an s1 follow-up and branchPattern is consumed by s6 (handoff). The three rows carry a note 'saved; not used yet' until then.

summary.prose: A developer sees and edits their own tracker settings for a repo (tracker type, target, the gh tool location and sign-in host, and branch naming) in VS Code, JetBrains and the terminal client, and sees the team's policy rules next to them as read-only values. All three clients render the same rows from one daemon definition and one read and write path over ~/.insrc/github.json, so a change made in one client shows in the others.

hldContextSlice.frameworkSummary: A daemon-side team gate over a synchronous, capability-declaring tracker port (alternative a1). The port (sc1) is the only way the workflow library talks to a tracker; GitHub is its first adapter, made by extracting the existing GitHub code (src/workflow/tracker, the issue calls in tracker-auto.ts, and the create and close calls in src/workflow/bugfix/tracker.ts) behind it. sc1 is the one tracker abstraction: the unbuilt tracker-tool design (LLD-38436e90625a83a2-S001) is not built as a second abstraction and is superseded or amended by s1's LLD. The policy (sc2) is read from the remote default branch and says which stages need signoff, whether claims are enforced, the claim units and the administrators. The artifact's tracker record keeps every existing meta.tracker field exactly as it is and gains additive per-unit data, plus an optional meta.revision (sc3). The team gate (sc4) takes a guarded action and returns an outcome. Signoff is a separate record (sc5) that never changes meta.review or approvedAt. Syncing tracker status on git pull and push, and the issue-status read it needs, are deferred with the later-tracker work to a define extend and are not part of this HLD.

consumedContracts.name: TeamPolicy
consumedContracts.purpose: The central rules read from the remote default branch: team mode, signoff stages, claim enforcement, claim units, administrators, and the grandfathering anchor. Owned by s2.

boundary.internal: The repo-scoped kind of row in the shared settings catalog whose reads and writes go to the per-repo map in github.json read by resolveGithubConfig; its rendering in VS Code, JetBrains and the terminal client; read-only display of policy values. Shares the single store with s1's target resolution.

adjacentBoundaries.internal: The GitHub adapter built by extracting src/workflow/tracker (including the existing signed-in-user read, ghCurrentLogin, behind whoAmI), the issue calls in tracker-auto.ts and the create and close calls in src/workflow/bugfix/tracker.ts behind the port; the gh command wrapper with its 10-second timeout; contract tests; detection of a missing tool or sign-in. The port receives the needed capabilities as an argument, so s1 does not read the policy. Reconciliation: the unbuilt tracker-tool design LLD-38436e90625a83a2-S001 (docs/standalone/add-add-items-tracker-setting-have-E2026100638436e90/S001/LLD.md) is not built as a second abstraction; sc1 is the one tracker abstraction and s1's LLD supersedes or amends that LLD, once its conflicting approval status is settled. Syncing tracker status on git pull and push, and an issue-status read on the port, are deferred to the define extend.

Reading the policy file from the remote default branch ref, the cached last-fetched copy and the offline rule, finding the first default-branch commit that carried the policy file, the starter policy and the team setup command.

Shared issue-creation code refactored out of autoPushEpicOnHld, autoPushStoryOnLld and autoPushTasksOnPlan, find-by-label dedupe for Story and Task issues, forcing Task issues on in team mode, daemon-side triggering when a draft is first written, the terminal approve path kept as manual fallback, the inventory and classification of artifact write paths (including the two writeFileSync writers, and both verdicts.ts and run-artifact.ts as content writes when auto-fixes change the body), the single content-write helper and the revision minting, the bypass test that also detects raw writeFileSync on artifact paths, and the rule that an artifact without meta.revision reads as revision 0.

The team gate and its call sites (daemon step entry points and approveArtifactByJsonPath), the acting-user read through the port, claim and release commands, live assignee reads, the guarded-action list (code-review and analyze are never guarded; review is never refused), the report-only review for a non-holder through the review-fix decision on both review paths (verdicts.ts and run-artifact.ts), the typed TeamGateRefusedError, its handling beside ReviewBlockedError in approveWorkflowTarget and its formatting in the terminal client's approve case in src/cli/command.ts, the no-issue outcome handling, administrator release, and the declaration of the completion hook, shipped unregistered.
Parking a draft on a handoff branch, the issue note, resuming from committed files, and reconstructing in-flight workflow state from committed artifacts instead of the opaque token.

Opening the signoff request with the chosen artifacts, prerequisite checks for model review and local approval, registering the completion hook to produce the awaiting-signoff outcome, the on-demand completion check, automatic release of the claim on completion, recording sign-off together, grandfathering of artifacts approved before the policy anchor, and the separate display of signoff.
Revision of an open request: re-run of local approval, push to the same request, discarding an earlier completion, refusing non-holders.
Private implementation of s9: Keep tracker issues and status in step with the work without a manual step

hldContextSlice.rolloutPhase: Phase B — settings and issue readiness

nonFunctional.performance: Each guarded action makes at most two live reads through the port (the signed-in user and the assignee); every tracker command has a 10-second timeout, after which the action is refused with the reason. A repo without a policy makes no tracker call.
nonFunctional.security: Policy is read only from the remote default branch ref and is not locally overridable; enforcement lives in the daemon-owned workflow library (k1); no tracker secrets are stored by insrc, sign-in stays with the tracker's CLI; administrators come only from the policy.
nonFunctional.observability: Every gate outcome other than allowed is logged with unit, action and reason; port failures carry their kind (missing-tool, missing-signin, unreachable, rejected).
nonFunctional.durability: Claim, issue and signoff state live in the tracker and in committed artifact files; the in-memory step state stores (100 entries, 1 hour) are not relied on for handoff. Artifact writes stay atomic through the existing helper.

dataModelChanges.details: The one definition table of the repo-scoped rows, in src/config next to CONFIG_CATALOG. Each row: key, label, type ('string' | 'boolean' | 'enum'), enumValues, default, description, group 'Tracker', and kind: 'local' (editable, stored in github.json), 'status' (derived, read-only: sign-in status of gh and the resolved target with its source) or 'policy' (read-only, from sc2). Local rows: type (github | none), owner, repo, ghPath (tool location of the gh program), ghHost (the GitHub host gh is signed in to, for GitHub Enterprise; default github.com), branchPattern (branch naming, with {id} {slug} {type} placeholders). Policy rows: teamMode, signoffStages, claimsEnforced, administrators, forceTaskIssues.
Adds repoFields: readonly RepoFieldDef[], the rows of REPO_TRACKER_FIELDS without values. Additive: clients that ignore it are unaffected.

{ repo: string; values: Record<string, string | boolean>; resolved: { type: 'github' | 'none'; owner?: string; repo?: string; source: 'per-repo-config' | 'default-config' | 'git-remote'; error?: string }; signin: { state: 'signed-in' | 'missing-tool' | 'missing-signin' | 'unreachable' | 'unknown'; login?: string }; policy: { ok: true; mode: 'none' } | { ok: true; mode: 'team'; values: Record<string, unknown>; source: { ref: string; fetchedAt: string } } | { ok: false; reason: string } }. 'values' holds only keys the repo's own entry sets; the resolved block is what resolveGithubConfig reports (ac12).

Adds optional ghPath, ghHost and branchPattern (strings). resolveGithubConfig, loadGithubConfigFile and resolveStrictTrackerTarget ignore them, so a repo without them resolves exactly as today (k4). The tool location and host are read by the gh runner only in a later story; this story stores and shows them.
dataModelChanges.schemaDiff: + readonly ghPath?: string; + readonly ghHost?: string; + readonly branchPattern?: string;

dataModelChanges.details: One writer module (readRepoEntry and writeRepoEntryKey) that parses the file, merges one key into repos[repo], and replaces the file atomically; used by repo.settings.set and by the config step of tracker setup so the file has a single writer path.

interactionWithShared.howDetails: repo.settings.get calls PolicyReader(repo) once and maps TeamPolicy to read-only rows: teamMode, signoffStages, claimsEnforced, administrators, forceTaskIssues, with source.ref and source.fetchedAt shown as where the value came from. No policy key can be written: repo.settings.set refuses any key whose kind is not 'local'. TeamPolicy is not changed and nothing is cached by this story.

errorCases.scenario: github.json exists but is not valid JSON or its top level is not an object
errorCases.detection: The read path in the github.json writer parses the file with JSON.parse and checks the result is a non-array object; a parse error or a wrong shape is caught there.
errorCases.response: repo.settings.get and repo.settings.set return github-json-unreadable naming the file and the parse error; set writes nothing and leaves the file untouched. The lenient resolver keeps its own behaviour (treats the file as empty).
errorCases.userImpact: The client shows the error and an offer to fix the file by hand; no setting is lost or overwritten.

errorCases.scenario: Two clients write at nearly the same time
errorCases.detection: All writes pass through one in-daemon queue, so two repo.settings.set calls never interleave; a write by a process other than the daemon (the terminal setup step before it is moved onto the writer) is detected by comparing the file's mtime and size read at the start of the merge with those just before the rename.
errorCases.response: The queued writes apply one after the other, each merging into the latest file. If the file changed between read and rename, the merge is redone once from the new content; if it changes again the call returns file-changed and writes nothing.
errorCases.userImpact: Both edits survive, or the second client is asked to retry; neither silently overwrites the other.

errorCases.scenario: A client sends a write for a policy or status row
errorCases.detection: repo.settings.set looks the key up in REPO_TRACKER_FIELDS and checks kind === 'local'.
errorCases.userImpact: The row is shown read-only in every client, so this only happens from a hand-made call; the value cannot be changed locally (k5).

errorCases.scenario: A value does not match its row (an enum outside its values, an owner or repo that is not a valid GitHub name, a branch pattern with an unknown placeholder, a ghPath that contains a newline)
errorCases.detection: repo.settings.set validates the value against the row's type, enumValues and format before any file access.
errorCases.response: Returns invalid-value with the reason; nothing is written.
errorCases.userImpact: The client shows the reason next to the field and keeps the old value.

errorCases.scenario: The repo is not registered with the daemon
errorCases.detection: Both methods look the path up in the repo registry before reading or writing.
errorCases.response: Returns repo-not-registered; no file is read or written.
errorCases.userImpact: The client's repo picker only lists registered repos, so this appears only after a repo is removed while the settings are open.

errorCases.scenario: The policy cannot be read (offline, no default branch known, malformed policy file)
errorCases.detection: PolicyReader returns ok:false and repo.settings.get checks the result.
errorCases.response: The payload carries policy: { ok: false, reason }; the local rows are still returned.
errorCases.userImpact: The policy section shows the reason instead of values; editing the local rows is unaffected.

errorCases.scenario: gh is not installed or not signed in when the sign-in status is computed
errorCases.detection: The status row uses the s1 classified runner and reads GhCommandError.kind (missing-tool, missing-signin, unreachable).
errorCases.response: signin.state is set to that kind with no login; the call does not fail and uses the 10-second timeout.
errorCases.userImpact: The sign-in row says what is missing and how to fix it (gh auth login), without blocking the settings view.

errorCases.scenario: github is enabled for the repo but no target can be resolved (type github, no owner/repo, git remote not parseable)
errorCases.detection: resolveGithubConfig throws GithubConfigError, caught in repo.settings.get.
errorCases.response: resolved.error carries the message and resolved.type is 'none'; the call succeeds.
errorCases.userImpact: The target row shows why there is no target and which fields to set.

errorCases.scenario: An older client calls config.catalog and does not know repoFields
errorCases.detection: The field is additive; the client simply does not read it.
errorCases.response: No change in what the client receives for existing fields.
errorCases.userImpact: The older client shows no tracker section until it is updated; nothing else changes.

alternativesConsidered.name: Repo settings payload and write over their own IPC pair, one field table
alternativesConsidered.oneLineSummary: A single field table in src/config describes the repo-scoped rows; two new daemon methods read the payload (editable local values plus read-only policy values) and write one field to github.json; all three clients render from the payload.
alternativesConsidered.approach: Add one definition site, a REPO_TRACKER_FIELDS table next to CONFIG_CATALOG: each row has a key, type, enum values, default, description and a kind of 'local' (editable) or 'policy' (read-only). Add a pure buildRepoSettings(repoPath, fileContent, policyResult) that returns the rows with the repo's current value, the resolved source of the target (own entry, default entry or git remote) and, for policy rows, the policy value with its source. Add two daemon IPC methods: repo.settings.get(repo) returns that payload, and repo.settings.set(repo, key, value) validates the key and value against the table, refuses a policy key, and writes only that repo's entry in github.json through a single atomic writer (read, merge, write to temp, rename) that also keeps the default entry untouched. VS Code, JetBrains and the terminal client render rows from the payload, so a field added to the table appears in all three. The new fields (tool location, sign-in note, branch naming) are added to GithubEntry as optional, so resolveGithubConfig and s1's strict resolver ignore them.
pros: One definition of the fields, so the three clients cannot drift (FR2, ac13)
Does not touch config.write or config.json, so the existing model-tier settings are unaffected
Reuses the github.json store that s1's resolution reads, so a change is seen by the next tracker resolution
Policy values and their source travel in the same payload, so ac14 needs no extra client logic
cons: Two new daemon methods and a new atomic writer for github.json
The IDE plugins and the terminal client each need a new section, though they render from one payload
The writer must keep the file's other repos and the default entry intact under concurrent edits from two clients

alternativesConsidered.name: Generalise config.catalog and config.write with a store selector
alternativesConsidered.oneLineSummary: Keep one catalog and one write method, and add a 'store' dimension so the same calls can address github.json per-repo entries as well as config.json.
alternativesConsidered.approach: Extend ConfigOption with an optional scope of 'repo' and a store of 'github.json', add a repoPath parameter to config.catalog and config.write, and branch inside buildSettingsCatalog and the write handler on the store. Repo-scoped rows live in CONFIG_CATALOG beside the daemon-wide rows. Policy rows are added to the same payload with a read-only flag.
pros: The smallest change in the clients if they already render the catalog generically
One catalog and one pair of methods for every setting
No new IPC method names to keep in step across the three clients
cons: config.write is path-based and global: adding a repo path and a second file widens a method used by every model-tier setting, and a mistake there can corrupt config.json
The catalog is pure and total over one raw object; making it read a second file and the policy breaks that property and its tests
buildSettingsCatalog would now depend on s2's policy reader, coupling the catalog to the workflow library
alternativesConsidered.reasonRejected: Closest to k6 but widens a global write path and breaks the catalog's purity and totality (partial on ac14, sc2 and k4).

alternativesConsidered.name: Each client owns its tracker form and talks to github.json through a thin read and write
alternativesConsidered.oneLineSummary: Add only a raw read and a raw write of a repo entry to the daemon, and let each client define its own fields and validation.
alternativesConsidered.approach: Add repo.githubEntry.get and repo.githubEntry.set that move the entry JSON as is, with the daemon checking only that it is an object. VS Code, JetBrains and the terminal client each hard-code the tracker fields, their labels and their validation.
pros: Clients can lay the form out as suits their toolkit
cons: Three copies of the field list and validation, which is exactly the drift the story forbids (FR2)
A client bug can write an invalid entry that s1's strict resolver then refuses
Policy values would need a third method and per-client handling
alternativesConsidered.reasonRejected: Violates the one-definition rule (k6) and leaves validation to three clients.
